question: To what extent was the Great Depression responsible for the Nazi Party's rise to power in Germany by January 1933?
subject: History
model_answer:
The Nazi Party's rise to power between the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 and Hitler's appointment as Chancellor on 30 January 1933 had two parts: the growth of a fringe party into the largest in the Reichstag, and the decision of the conservative elite around President Hindenburg to hand it the chancellorship. The Great Depression was responsible for the first almost entirely and for the second only in part. It was the necessary condition without which neither would have happened, but it was not sufficient: the structural weaknesses of the Weimar constitution and the choices made by the elite in 1932 and January 1933 decided that the Depression produced Hitler rather than another outcome. The Depression created the Nazi electorate, destroyed parliamentary government, and so brought Hitler to the threshold of power; it was the elite that carried him across it.

The Depression was responsible, first, for creating the mass electorate without which the Nazi Party would have remained marginal. Registered unemployment rose from about 1.4 million in 1928 to more than six million by early 1932, and the Nazi vote rose with it: from 2.6 per cent and twelve seats in May 1928, to 18.3 per cent and 107 seats in September 1930, to 37.3 per cent and 230 seats in July 1932, when the party became the largest in the Reichstag. The correlation is not itself the explanation; the mechanism was that the Depression destroyed the security of groups that had previously voted for the moderate and conservative parties. The agrarian crisis that had begun in 1928 ruined the Protestant farming north, so that Schleswig-Holstein gave the Nazis an absolute majority of 51 per cent in July 1932, and the small-business Mittelstand, threatened with ruin and frightened by a Communist vote that grew from 10.6 per cent in 1928 to 16.9 per cent in November 1932, turned to a party that promised national community and the destruction of Marxism. The Depression mattered because it gave the Nazi message an audience that had not existed in 1928. The counter-case is that the unemployed themselves voted more often for the Communists than for the Nazis, and that the Nazi vote fell to 33.1 per cent in November 1932 as the economy showed its first signs of recovery, which suggests that distress alone did not translate into Nazi votes. The fall, however, came only after the Depression had already made the party the largest in Germany; by the criterion of what made the breakthrough possible, the Depression was decisive even if it did not fix the exact size of the vote. Economic collapse was therefore responsible for the Nazi Party's electoral rise to a degree no other factor matched.

The Depression was responsible, second, for the collapse of parliamentary government, which created the presidential politics through which Hitler could be appointed. The last majority government, Hermann Müller's grand coalition, broke apart in March 1930 over the deficit in the unemployment insurance fund, a dispute the Depression had created, and his successor Heinrich Brüning governed by emergency decree under Article 48 after the Reichstag rejected his budget in July 1930. In 1932 the Reichstag passed five laws while sixty-six emergency decrees were issued, which shows how completely law-making had passed from parliament to the President and his advisers. This shift mattered because it meant that by 1932 the chancellorship no longer depended on a Reichstag majority but on Hindenburg's signature, so that a leader who could never have assembled a majority could be appointed by a handful of men. Brüning's deflationary policy deepened the slump and discredited democratic government, and the election he provoked in September 1930 gave the Nazis their breakthrough. Against this, the weaknesses the Depression exploited were older than the Depression: Article 48, proportional representation and an elite that had never accepted the republic were all in place in 1919, and historians who stress these structural flaws argue that the Depression activated them rather than created them. The distinction is right but does not shift the weight: a constitution with such flaws had survived the crisis of 1923, and it was the economic collapse after 1929 that turned latent weaknesses into the actual rule by decree that made January 1933 possible. The Depression was therefore responsible for the form of government that could appoint Hitler, if not for the flaws that made that form available.

The Depression was not, finally, responsible for the decision to make Hitler Chancellor, which belonged to the conservative elite. By the end of 1932 the Nazi movement was faltering: Hitler had lost the presidential election to Hindenburg in April 1932 by 36.8 per cent to 53 per cent; Hindenburg had refused him the chancellorship on 13 August 1932 despite the 230 seats won in July; the vote fell in November; party finances were strained; and in December Gregor Strasser's resignation from his party offices exposed a movement in crisis. The appointment of 30 January 1933 came not from this ebbing electoral tide but from Franz von Papen's intrigue against Chancellor Schleicher, in which Papen persuaded Hindenburg that a cabinet with only three Nazis, Papen as Vice-Chancellor and conservatives in the other posts could use Hitler's mass following while controlling him. This mattered because it shows that at the moment of decision the Depression's electoral effect was receding and the outcome depended on calculation by a few men; one historian of those weeks has argued that Hitler's appointment was the contingent result of intrigue in January 1933, and others describe the elite's belief that it could control him as a miscalculation. The counter-case is strong: without the Depression there would have been no 230 seats for Papen to want to harness, and Schleicher's attempt to split the Nazi Party failed because the mass base the Depression had built was still there. By the criterion of necessity the Depression remains the precondition even of the intrigue; by the criterion of sufficiency it fails, because the men who held power in January 1933 could have chosen otherwise and nearly did. The Depression made Hitler possible; the elite made him Chancellor.

The Great Depression was therefore responsible for the Nazi rise to power to a large extent, but not wholly. It was the decisive precondition: without it the party would have remained the fringe movement of 1928, and parliamentary government would not have given way to rule by decree. It explains why the Nazi Party reached the threshold of power. It does not alone explain why the threshold was crossed, because the appointment of January 1933 required the inherited weaknesses of the Weimar constitution and a miscalculation by the conservative elite that the Depression made likely but did not compel. The Depression was necessary; it was not sufficient.
